name: Sulfur (topical)

lead: Topical sulfur is one of the oldest skin treatments, sold over the counter in washes, masks and spot treatments. People use it to get fewer breakouts, less redness and clearer skin, especially if they want to avoid harsher actives.

Sulfur is described as keratolytic and antimicrobial, so it helps clear pores and cut bacteria. Dermatology reviews list sulfur with sodium sulfacetamide among rosacea therapies backed by more than one randomised trial; for acne alone, the available sources include a label and a comedogenicity study but fewer controlled trials.

paras: It comes as a wash, mask or leave-on spot treatment, applied to breakout-prone areas or the whole face, often as a gentler alternative to stronger acne actives. Users generally treat it as part of an ongoing routine and judge results over several weeks.

OTC acne products carry external-use-only warnings. A randomised study found no link between sulfur and comedone formation under its conditions, and trials in scabies and hand eczema did not highlight prominent adverse effects. Sulfur products can smell strongly and may dry or irritate skin.

angle.text: Topical sulfur is an over-the-counter option in masks, soaps and spot treatments for acne, rosacea and body breakouts. Its antibacterial, keratolytic action leads to fewer breakouts and less redness, which shows as clearer skin. Rosacea trials have tested it combined with sodium sulfacetamide.

lead: Topical sulfur is one of the oldest skin treatments in use, sold in lotions, creams, soaps, masks, bath additives and dab-on spot treatments. People use it chiefly to dry out and reduce pimples, to calm the papules and pustules of rosacea, and to manage flaking from seborrhoeic dermatitis, all of which show on the face as clearer, calmer, less red skin.[1][2]

The sulfur in skin products is usually precipitated sulfur, a fine yellow powder. It is commonly described as keratolytic (it loosens and sheds surface skin cells) and antimicrobial, effects attributed to hydrogen sulfide that forms when sulfur interacts with skin cells and bacteria.[2] In the United States, sulfur acne treatments are sold over the counter, and a widely used prescription form pairs 5 percent sulfur with sodium sulfacetamide for rosacea and acne.[1][3]

Research includes two 2005 Cutis reviews that list sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide among rosacea therapies backed by more than one randomised trial, a 2023 Japanese real-world comparison with metronidazole, randomised trials in scabies and hand eczema, and a 1978 study of whether sulfur causes comedones.[4][5][6][7][8][9] A 2025 narrative review of sulfur in dermatology describes its mechanisms as under-studied and calls for more preclinical work.[10]
infobox: Octasulfur (S8); precipitated, colloidal or sublimed sulfur[2]
OTC in the US for acne (labelled products); prescription for sulfur/sulfacetamide combinations[1][3]
Sulfur 5 percent with sodium sulfacetamide, marketed as Plexion, Clenia, Prascion, Avar[3]

paras: Topical sulfur appears in three overlapping product families: over-the-counter acne washes, masks and spot treatments; prescription sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide lotions, washes and foams; and sulfur ointments for scabies. Which one a person meets depends on the problem, but the appearance goal is similar: fewer blemishes, less shine and flaking, and calmer colour.[1][3]

A US over-the-counter spot treatment label lists sulfur for the treatment of acne and carries a for-external-use-only warning.[1] Acne products often combine sulfur with other agents, and a registered phase 4 study compared medications containing benzoyl peroxide and sulfur in moderate acne; its status is listed as unknown.[11] The general acne literature describes benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid as the more commonly studied over-the-counter agents, and notes that acne treatments typically take 8 to 12 weeks to show results.[12]

Sulfur has an unusual comedogenicity history. A 1978 study by Strauss, Goldman, Nacht and Gans in Archives of Dermatology, run by two investigators at separate institutions with groups of 12 and 40 subjects, applied a 5 percent sulfur patch in two vehicles and took biopsies before and after six weeks. It found no link between sulfur and comedone formation, and reported that one of the vehicles (Triton X-100) itself appeared comedogenic.[8]

Two 2005 reviews in Cutis listed topical sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide, alongside metronidazole, azelaic acid and oral tetracyclines, among rosacea therapies supported by more than one randomised controlled trial.[4][5] The sulfur/sulfacetamide combinations are commonly promoted for rosacea with papules and pustules.[3]

A 2023 retrospective study in JMA Journal reviewed records of 47 Japanese patients treated for at least eight weeks with a topical sulfur preparation or topical metronidazole. Severity and symptom scores improved in nearly all subgroups, and improvement and adverse-event rates did not differ significantly between the two preparations.[9] Rosacea references also describe metronidazole, azelaic acid and ivermectin as other topical options.[13]
Sulfur is listed among agents used for seborrhoeic dermatitis, which presents as red, flaking skin around the nose, brows and scalp, and sodium sulfacetamide lotions are labelled for it.[2][3]

Sulfur ointments are an older treatment for scabies. The Japanese Dermatological Association guideline notes that sulfur preparations were the only topical scabies drugs covered by national health insurance there while describing their usefulness as limited, and reviews of scabies in resource-limited settings list sulfur alongside ivermectin and benzyl benzoate.[14][15] A randomised comparison in 97 Iraqi patients tested 8 and 10 percent sulfur ointment under different application schedules.[6] In a 2024 triple-blind trial in 70 patients with hand eczema, 2 percent sulfur cream and 0.1 percent triamcinolone cream both lowered severity scores over four weeks.[7]

Wikipedia's pharmacy article distinguishes flowers of sulfur (unpurified sublimed sulfur), purified sulfur washed with ammonia, precipitated sulfur made by boiling sulfur with lime and precipitating with acid, and colloidal sulfur, a very fine greyish-white powder. Precipitated sulfur is the form used in topical acne and dermatitis products.[2]

Consumer products include soaps, bar cleansers, clay and sulfur masks, and leave-on spot treatments. Prescription products combine sulfur at 5 percent with sodium sulfacetamide, a sulfonamide antibiotic, and are sold under names such as Plexion, Clenia, Prascion and Avar.[3] Lime sulfur, a different preparation of calcium polysulfides, is used in agriculture and in diluted form as a pet dip; it is not the same as the sulfur in acne products.[16]

Sulfur is reduced to hydrogen sulfide, partly by bacteria, and the hydrogen sulfide is credited with killing bacteria including Propionibacterium acnes, as well as fungi and scabies mites. The same gas, produced by keratinocytes in contact with sulfur, is described as the source of its keratolytic (peeling, skin-softening) effect.[2]

The 2025 narrative review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology describes sulfur as having broad-spectrum antimicrobial and immunomodulatory activity, covers indications such as scabies, tinea versicolor, psoriasis and atopic dermatitis, and identifies gaps in understanding of the bioactivity of sulfur and its derivatives, including hydrogen sulfide.[10]

Over-the-counter labels advise external use only.[1] The most common effects are irritation at the application site such as dryness, stinging, itching and peeling; rare generalised allergic reactions have been described, and swallowing large amounts can cause hydrogen sulfide poisoning, a risk that topical use rarely approaches except when large amounts are applied to small children.[2] The characteristic odor comes from sulfur compounds.[2]

Sodium sulfacetamide products carry additional considerations: they are not for people sensitive to sulfa drugs, and rare severe skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome have been reported with the drug.[3] The comedogenicity study found no association between sulfur and comedone formation under its conditions, and a scabies trial and a hand eczema trial reported efficacy outcomes without prominent adverse effects in the available abstracts.[7][6][8]

Sulfur is among the older ingredients in the skincare aisle and is commonly sold alongside newer actives in drugstore acne lines. The 2025 review notes that drug administrations in most regions set usage restrictions and regulations for sulfur products, which it summarises for the first time.[10] Among appearance-focused communities, discussion of topical products tends to centre on retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, minoxidil and peptides; sulfur is mentioned less often as a budget spot treatment.

Randomised and controlled evidence includes: sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide for rosacea, summarised in two reviews;[4][5] a 1978 comedogenicity study in 52 subjects across two institutions;[8] an RCT in scabies (97 patients) comparing application regimens of 8 and 10 percent sulfur ointment;[6] and a 70-patient RCT in hand eczema finding 2 percent sulfur cream comparable to 0.1 percent triamcinolone over four weeks, with benefits lasting through follow-up.[7] A 2023 retrospective study of 47 rosacea patients compared sulfur and metronidazole preparations.[9] A registered acne trial combining sulfur with benzoyl peroxide has unknown status.[11] Evidence specific to sulfur as a standalone acne treatment is limited to these items.

lore.intro: Online skincare discussion treats sulfur as a traditional, inexpensive spot treatment and mask ingredient, usually mentioned alongside benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid.[12]
